title: Corn Rust: How to Spot It and Protect Your Mais
metaTitle: Corn Rust: Signs, Damage and Control in Mais
metaDescription: Corn rust makes powdery brown pustules on mais leaves in warm, wet weather. Learn to tell common from southern rust and when a spray is worth it.
excerpt: Corn rust is a fungal disease that covers mais leaves with small, powdery, rusty pustules. Two fungi cause it, Puccinia sorghi and Puccinia polysora, and the second one is more common in the tropics.

heroImage.alt: A corn leaf covered with small orange brown rust pustules
heroImage.credit: Daren Mueller, Iowa State University, Bugwood.org, CC BY 3.0 US, via Wikimedia Commons

blocks.text:
Corn rust comes in two kinds. Common rust is caused by Puccinia sorghi, and southern rust, also called American corn rust, is caused by Puccinia polysora. The Pacific Pests and Pathogens database says both are widespread across tropical and subtropical regions, and that southern rust is more common in the tropics, especially at low altitude.

For most Philippine corn growers, rust is a late season problem. It usually shows after the tassel opens, when the grain has already started to form. That is why the Pacific Pests fact sheet calls it usually of minor importance. Even so, a heavy attack in a susceptible hybrid can cut yield, so scout your field and read our [pagtatanim ng mais](/crops/pagtatanim-ng-mais) guide to time planting well.

blocks.caption: Quick facts
rows: Corn rust shows up late in the crop, around and after tasseling, and it spreads fastest in warm, wet weather.
The spores are powdery and the wind carries them from field to field. A pustule makes thousands of spores, and the fungus survives on crop debris and volunteer corn.

blocks.text: Look at both sides of the leaf. Common rust pustules are circular to elongate, powdery, and brown to brick red, scattered over both leaf surfaces. Southern rust pustules are round to oval, light cinnamon brown to orange, and packed in dense groups mostly on the upper surface. Rub a pustule with your finger. If it leaves rusty brown powder, it is rust.

items: Small, round to oval pustules on the leaves, brown, orange or brick red.
Powdery spores that rub off as rusty dust on your fingers or clothes.
Common rust pustules scattered on both sides of the leaf.
Southern rust pustules in dense clusters on the upper side of the leaf.
Pustules turning brown black as the plant ages, with leaves that dry early on bad attacks.

blocks.title: Do not confuse it with
blocks.text: Rust pustules are often mistaken for [corn downy mildew](/diseases/corn-downy-mildew) or [northern corn leaf blight](/diseases/northern-corn-leaf-blight). Rust leaves powder on your finger, blight makes long tan cigar shaped lesions, and downy mildew shows pale stripes and white fuzz on young plants.
How Corn Rust Hurts Your Corn

Common rust is minor on most modern corn hybrids, and the Pacific Pests fact sheet says it is a bigger worry for sweet corn. Southern rust is the more aggressive one. University of Nebraska extension reports losses of up to 45 percent in severe cases in the United States, and about 6 percent loss for each 10 percent of leaf area infected by common rust. Those are US figures, so Philippine losses will differ by variety and season.

A spray threshold from the Pacific Pests fact sheet is an average of six pustules per leaf on susceptible crops. Because the damage grows with warm, wet days, scouting every week from tasseling is the key. For a wider look at what attacks mais, see our guide to [crop pests in the Philippines](/pests/crop-pests-philippines).

items: Plant a resistant variety. The Pacific Pests fact sheet calls resistant varieties the best way to manage rust, and many hybrids carry it.
Plant in the drier season where you can, and avoid planting next to an infected field.
Destroy volunteer corn and bury or burn crop debris after harvest.
Remove Oxalis weeds near the field, because they can host common rust.
Plant early or use shorter season varieties so the crop matures before the disease peaks, as University of Nebraska extension advises.
Scout weekly from tasseling and decide on a spray only if the pustules are heavy and the weather stays wet.

blocks.text: A spray rarely pays on a field corn crop, because rust arrives late and the effect on yield is often minor. It can make sense on susceptible sweet corn or in a bad year. Rotate the fungicide group, because repeated use of one group can lead to resistant rust. Follow the FPA registered label.

blocks.caption: Active ingredients that work. Always follow the label of an FPA registered product.
rows: protectant, named by the Pacific Pests fact sheet, start at about six pustules per leaf

blocks.title: Spray safely
blocks.text: Use only products registered with the [Fertilizer and Pesticide Authority](/blog/fertilizer-and-pesticide-authority), and follow the label for the rate, the timing and the protective clothing. Switch to a different fungicide group next time, so the disease does not learn to survive it. Our [guide to plant diseases](/diseases/plant-diseases-philippines) explains how.

items: Choose a rust tolerant hybrid and check the seed label or ask your supplier.
Keep the field clean of volunteer corn and weeds that carry the fungus.
Plant on time with your neighbors, so the crop avoids the warm, wet peak.
Record the weeks rust appeared, then change your planting date next season.

blocks.text: Questions Farmers Ask About Corn Rust

items.q: What is the difference between common rust and southern rust?
items.a: Common rust (Puccinia sorghi) has brick red to brown pustules on both sides of the leaf and prefers cooler weather. Southern rust (Puccinia polysora) has orange to cinnamon pustules in dense groups on the upper side and likes warm weather.

items.q: Do I need to spray for corn rust?
items.a: Usually not on field corn, since rust arrives late and often costs little yield. Spray only on a susceptible crop with heavy pustules, using the label and rotating groups.

items.q: Can corn rust spread from one field to another?
items.a: Yes. The spores are powdery and the wind carries them far. That is why planting date and clearing volunteer corn matter. See our page on [corn seeds](/crops/corn-seeds) for choosing a variety.
